Index.sub hello: Discover quantum science and technology, explained at three levels.
Index.difficulty description: Whether you're a beginner, intermediate, or advanced learner, we have content tailored to your level.
Index.Difficulty Elementary 2: Perfect for beginners with no prior knowledge of quantum concepts.
Index.Difficulty High School 2: Designed for students with basic understanding of physics and mathematics.
Index.Difficulty College 2: Advanced content for university students and professionals.

About Us.motivation subtitle: Bridging the gap between quantum science and society through education, innovation, and collaboration
About Us.s1 p1: Quantum technology is usually described in one of two registers: Headlines that promise a revolution without explaining things precisely, or publications written for specialists. Readers who are curious but not yet experts often find little between the two.
About Us.s1 p2: We seek to provide an engaging space for everyone to learn about quantum technology, regardless of their prior knowledge. Hence WiQi was built.
About Us.s1 p3: You can find a variety of quantum subjects — be it entanglement, decoherence or superconductivity — on three levels: an easy, a medium and a difficult version. These are not three separate texts but one explanation at three depths. You may begin at whichever level suits you the most, and move up as your understanding grows.
About Us.s1 p4: Alongside these encyclopedia-like entries, WiQi also collects write-ups of the Quantum Tuesdays (Quantendienstag) lecture series at the Deutsches Museum, and a short glossary of quantum terminology under Quantum Alphabet. All of it is available in German and English, and all of it is freely accessible.
About Us.s2 p1: WiQi was developed within <qtr>Quanten(t)räume</qtr>, as a “digital twin” of the project. Quanten(t)räume is a collaborative science-communication project funded by the <bmftr>Federal Ministry of Research, Technology and Space</bmftr>, running from December 2023 to November 2026.
About Us.s2 p2: The project proceeds from the conviction that second-generation quantum technologies should be discussed rather than merely announced. Its partners develop outreach formats that connect to one another: museum exhibits, advanced courses in school laboratories, teacher training, public lectures, and games. Three overarching goals run through all of these formats:
About Us.s2 goal1: Creating networked spaces, online and at several locations, in which the public can learn about quantum technology, exchange views with one another and with specialists, and think through possible applications together.
About Us.s2 goal2: Supporting early-career researchers and vocational education through science-communication training, advanced courses at the PhotonLab school laboratory, school seminars and teacher training.
About Us.s2 goal3: Prompting dialogue between the general public and experts, and enabling both sides to learn from each other, to give researchers a concrete picture of how quantum technology is seen by the public.
About Us.s2 p3: Hence the purpose is not only to attract talent to the field, but to ensure that quantum technologies develop in step with what the public actually understands and wants.
About Us.s2 p4: WiQi is a written and lasting layer of this work, and aims to demystify quantum technology for the general public.
About Us.s3 p1: Quanten(t)räume is coordinated by the <dm>Deutsches Museum</dm> and carried out together with:
About Us.s3 partner1: Max Planck Institute of Quantum Optics (MPQ) — PhotonLab
About Us.s3 partner2: Fraunhofer Institute for Systems and Innovation Research (ISI)
About Us.s3 p2: <mcqst>MCQST</mcqst>, <iqm>IQM</iqm> and the <mqv>Munich Quantum Valley</mqv> are associated partners.
About Us.s4 p1: PushQuantum e.V. is a student initiative based in Munich, formed by students from the Technical University of Munich and Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität.
About Us.s4 p2: This initiative is community-driven: our members lead the projects they care about, supported by the network around them. Our work rests on three pillars: community, professional development, and outreach. WiQi belongs to the third, under the Quanten(t)räume project.
About Us.s4 p3: We believe that quantum science and technology have the potential to revolutionize our future. Thus, we are committed to equipping society with the knowledge and tools to prepare for and actively participate in this movement.

Applications.title: Quantum Applications
Applications.subtitle: Where quantum technologies are already changing our world
Applications.intro: Quantum technologies are being explored in medicine, communication, industry, and other fields. Some applications already exist in limited forms, while others are research concepts or laboratory demonstrations. This overview summarizes 16 technology profiles from the Deutsches Museum. The descriptions are paraphrased from those profiles; they are not claims that every technology is ready for everyday use.
Applications.sourceNote: The summaries are based on the Deutsches Museum's <link>Technology Profiles</link>, developed with Fraunhofer ISI. Each application page links to its individual profile.
Applications.moreDetails: Click here for the full Deutsches Museum article

summaries.prosthesis: Nerve signals produce tiny magnetic fields that are difficult to measure. The profile describes diamond sensors using nitrogen-vacancy (NV) centers, whose quantum states respond to magnetic fields and can be read with laser light. In the future, these measurements might help translate a person's movement intentions into more natural prosthesis or exoskeleton controls. The approach is still being developed.
summaries.cancer: This profile explores using hyperpolarization to make the magnetic-resonance signal from metabolism-related molecules much stronger. Researchers could then study how tissues use molecules such as pyruvate, potentially revealing changes in a tumour or showing whether treatment is working. The approach remains at the basic-research stage: the enhanced signal fades quickly, and the method is not yet a clinical screening tool.
summaries.drugs: Quantum simulations might help researchers model how molecules interact with drug targets, while quantum-based machine-learning methods are being explored for analysing research data. These tools could eventually help prioritize compounds for laboratory testing, but they do not replace experiments or clinical trials. Current quantum computers are not yet powerful and reliable enough for routine simulation of pharmaceutical-scale molecules, and a practical advantage remains to be demonstrated.
summaries.imaging: Some quantum-imaging methods use pairs of entangled photons: one photon interacts with an object, while its partner is detected to help form the image. In one approach described by the Museum, an object can be illuminated with infrared light while the image is detected using visible light, potentially avoiding a specialized infrared camera. Laboratory images have been demonstrated, but current systems are slow and have limited resolution.
summaries.cryptography: Quantum key distribution (QKD) uses quantum states of light to let two parties establish a shared encryption key and detect certain kinds of interception: measuring transmitted quantum states can disturb them. QKD distributes keys; it does not itself encrypt the message, and secure use also depends on properly implemented equipment and authenticated communication. Systems are available, but distance, cost, integration, and the lack of practical quantum repeaters limit wider networks.
summaries.internet: A quantum internet would connect quantum devices by distributing entanglement, enabling applications such as linking quantum computers, networked sensors, and specialized secure communication. It would not simply be a faster version of today's internet. Because quantum states cannot be copied like ordinary signals, long-distance links need quantum memories and repeaters. Small network demonstrations exist, but reliable, large-scale networks remain a research goal.
summaries.logistics: Planning delivery routes, timetables, or vehicle assignments involves many possible combinations and practical constraints. Quantum annealers and other quantum algorithms are being tested as part of hybrid workflows, where classical computers prepare and evaluate solutions. These systems may help explore difficult optimization problems, but logistics applications are still being tested, and a consistent advantage over strong classical optimization methods has not been established.
summaries.finance: Financial researchers are investigating quantum algorithms for tasks such as estimating portfolio risk, optimizing asset mixes, and analysing market data. One proposed route is to use quantum algorithms to reduce the number of samples needed in certain Monte Carlo estimates; another is to explore optimization methods for portfolios. Demonstrations so far use simplified problems, so practical gains in real financial systems remain uncertain.
summaries.weather: Quantum computers could eventually assist selected parts of weather modelling, such as data assimilation or solving large mathematical systems, while quantum sensors might provide more precise measurements for the models. Better forecasts could support preparation for storms, floods, and heatwaves. Today's quantum computers cannot run realistic global weather models; near-term progress may come from testing small computational tasks or improving measurements with sensors.
summaries.navigation: Atom-interferometry sensors can measure acceleration, rotation, or gravity and may support navigation when GPS signals are unavailable, such as underwater or in tunnels. Unlike conventional inertial systems, highly precise quantum sensors could reduce the accumulation of position error over time. Laboratory prototypes and field tests have been reported, but current devices need substantial miniaturization and protection from vibration and temperature changes.
summaries.gravimeters: Quantum gravimeters use laser-cooled atoms to detect tiny changes in gravity caused by underground differences in mass. The measurements could help locate groundwater, geological structures, or hidden cavities without drilling. The profile describes devices that have moved beyond laboratory research, including field demonstrations, but current instruments are still relatively large, costly, and sensitive to vibration.
summaries.batteries: Quantum batteries are a research concept for storing energy in the excited states of quantum systems rather than through ordinary chemical reactions. When many systems interact, collective effects such as superabsorption may—in theory—allow larger systems to absorb energy faster under suitable conditions. Laboratory experiments have begun to study these effects, but a practical rechargeable quantum battery is not yet available.
summaries.catalysis: Quantum computers might help model the electrons involved in catalytic reactions, potentially helping researchers understand how catalysts work and identify promising materials. The motivation includes industrial processes such as ammonia production, which currently require substantial energy. Relevant simulations remain difficult for today's quantum hardware, and any predicted catalyst would still need to be made and tested in a laboratory.
summaries.dots: Quantum dots are nanoscale semiconductor particles that confine electrons, giving them size-dependent energy levels and light-emission colours. They are already used in QLED displays; other proposed uses include biological imaging, solar cells, and quantum-computing qubits. The maturity varies by application, and biomedical use requires careful attention to material safety because some quantum dots contain toxic elements.
summaries.ai: Quantum machine learning explores whether quantum computers can help with selected data-analysis or model-training tasks; conversely, AI methods may help control and calibrate quantum devices. Potential research areas include chemistry, materials, and complex datasets. The field is active, but a clear advantage over well-optimized classical machine learning on practical tasks has not yet been established.
summaries.transistors: A single-atom transistor uses an individual atom to form or interrupt a conducting connection between tiny contacts. At this scale, electrical conductance follows quantum rules and can change in discrete steps. Laboratory prototypes have demonstrated switching, suggesting a possible route to very small, low-energy electronics. Reliable atom placement, long-term stability, and manufacturing at chip scale remain major engineering challenges.

Partners.title: The People and Partners Behind Quantum Outreach
Partners.subtitle: Meet the organizations connecting quantum research, technology, and people
Partners.intro: Quantum technologies start with scientific discoveries. To help people understand what they could mean in everyday life, it is useful to bring together researchers, technology experts, museums, and educators. Meet the organizations whose work connects these different perspectives.
Partners.mpq name: Max Planck Institute of Quantum Optics (MPQ)
Partners.mpq text: Based in Garching near Munich, the <link>Max Planck Institute of Quantum Optics</link> studies how light and matter behave. This research helps scientists understand the basic ideas behind quantum technologies.
Partners.mpq alt: Max Planck Institute of Quantum Optics logo
Partners.isi name: Fraunhofer Institute for Systems and Innovation Research (Fraunhofer ISI)
Partners.isi text: The <link>Fraunhofer Institute for Systems and Innovation Research</link> looks at how new ideas and technologies develop, and how they affect people, businesses, and the environment. Its work helps us think about both what new technologies can do and how they might change our lives.
Partners.isi alt: Fraunhofer Institute for Systems and Innovation Research logo
Partners.dm text: The <link>Deutsches Museum</link> helps visitors explore science and technology through exhibitions and learning activities. Its <profiles>quantum technology profiles</profiles> show how quantum ideas could be used, for example, in navigation and secure communication.
Partners.technoseum text: The <link>TECHNOSEUM in Mannheim</link> explores how technology and society have changed over time. Its exhibitions and hands-on activities invite visitors to discover how technology connects with everyday life.
Partners.pq text: <link>PushQuantum</link> is a student-led initiative that makes quantum technologies easier to understand. It creates learning materials and activities for people with different backgrounds, helping more people explore quantum science.
Partners.closing text: Together, these organizations bring research, new ideas, museums, and education into the same conversation. Their work helps people explore quantum technologies as both scientific discoveries and possible tools for the future.
